plan.topic: What is 'dysesthesia', the retatrutide side effect in the new head-to-head trial? How often it happened against semaglutide 2 mg (TRANSCEND-T2D-2, Lilly, Oct 28, 2026)
plan.angle: 20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question rather than re-cutting the long-form. Answer within 10 s: 'Dysesthesia means odd skin sensations, like tingling or burning. In Lilly's new trial in type 2 diabetes, it was reported in 4.8% on retatrutide 9 mg and 6.5% on 12 mg, versus 2.7% on semaglutide 2 mg, over 80 weeks.' Credit it 'Lilly, Oct 28, 2026; company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed; open-label'. Use numbers that match L1's verified script exactly. Second fact: more people stopped retatrutide because of side effects (4.8% / 7.9% vs 2.7%), while stomach side effects were broadly similar to semaglutide. Give one per-arm nausea figure. Honest uncertainty: the cause isn't known. Status: investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 29, 2026. Never mention online products; for approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. Last spoken line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' No spoken titles. 170 words or fewer. Mix at 0.02 or lower.

package.title: Retatrutide's Skin-Sensation Side Effect: What Is Dysesthesia? #shorts
package.description:
Dysesthesia means unusual or unpleasant skin sensations, like burning, or touch that feels painful. In Lilly's 80-week open-label trial of ~1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes, dysesthesia was reported in 4.8% on retatrutide 9mg, 6.5% on 12mg, vs 2.7% on semaglutide 2mg. More people stopped retatrutide for side effects (4.8% and 7.9% vs 2.7%); diarrhea and nausea were most common, and severity wasn't reported in this trial. Company-reported Oct 28, 2026, not yet peer-reviewed; retatrutide is investigational, not approved anywhere.

Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
Lilly press release, 28 Oct 2026: https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/lillys-retatrutide-delivered-greater-a1c-reduction-and-more-than-double-the-weight-loss-of-ozempics-highest-approved-dose-in-head-to-head-trial
NCI definition: https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/dysesthesia

factcheck.summary:
I checked every number in this Short against Lilly's 28 Oct 2026 press release on BioSpace and against HCPLive's coverage, and they all match. The trial is TRANSCEND-T2D-2: 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes, 80 weeks, randomized and open-label, retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg versus semaglutide 2 mg.
- Dysesthesia: 4.8% on 9 mg, 6.5% on 12 mg and 2.7% on semaglutide.
- Stopping because of side effects: 4.8%, 7.9% and 2.7%.
- Lilly's release says nothing about how severe the dysesthesia was or what causes it, so "not reported" is accurate.
- Lilly Medical's TRIUMPH page confirms the obesity-trial events were "mostly mild to moderate in severity" and that dysesthesia was defined as skin burning and related events.
- The NCI definition (touch distorted, so an ordinary stimulus feels unpleasant or painful) supports the plain-English wording.
- The release says retatrutide is not approved by FDA or any other regulator.

Labels ("company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed, open-label"), the safety lines and the CTA all follow the rules. I found three minor things to fix:
1. The narration runs to about 171 words, just over the 170 cap.
2. In s6, diarrhea on 12 mg (32.7% vs 26.4%) isn't really "close" to semaglutide.
3. One source in the list (s4) isn't cited by any scene and I couldn't open it.

issues.claim: Diarrhea and nausea were the most common side effects, at rates close to semaglutide's.
issues.problem: Nausea was close (21.2% and 23.8% vs 21.3%), but diarrhea on 12 mg was 32.7% vs 26.4%. That's about 6 points higher, so 'close' overstates how similar the arms were. The whole Short is also at about 171 spoken words, over the 170-word limit.
issues.fix: Replace the first sentence of s6 with: "Diarrhea and nausea were the most common side effects in every arm." (This is accurate: they were the top two on retatrutide 9 mg, 12 mg and semaglutide. It also brings the Short down to about 168 words.)

issues.claim: Severity not reported in this trial
issues.problem: Muted viewers see only the missing-severity point and not the scoped obesity-trial context, so the screen text is narrower than the narration. That's an inconsistency, not a misleading claim.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "Severity not reported here; mostly mild–moderate in obesity trials (Lilly)"

issues.problem: No scene cites it, and I couldn't open the page to confirm its contents (it loads with JavaScript). The press release does confirm the NCT number.
issues.fix: Remove s4 from the source list, or keep it only as a background reference without using it to credit any line.
